e.etymology: A spelling of Aaliyah, the feminine of Arabic Ali (high, exalted). The same sound is the Hebrew word aliyah (ascent). The singer Aaliyah made the name popular in the US from the mid-1990s.
A double-n spelling of Viviana, the Latin, Italian and Spanish form of Vivian, from Latin vivus (alive). Saint Viviana, also called Bibiana, was a 4th-century Roman martyr.
From an English surname, a variant of Deighton, a Yorkshire place name from Old English dic (ditch, dike) plus tun (settlement). Dayton, Ohio, takes its name from the surname.

assoc.t: Dayton, Ohio, hometown of the Wright brothers

e.etymology: From an English surname that began as a medieval form of the given name Hilary, from Latin hilaris (cheerful), or of Eulalie. Ellery Queen, the detective and pen name created in 1929, made it familiar in America.
namesakes: Ellery Queen (fictional detective and mystery-writing pen name)

e.meaning: peace; in Scandinavia, beautiful or beloved
e.etymology: In Scandinavia, from Old Norse Frida, short for names ending in fridr (beautiful, beloved); in German-speaking Europe, a short form of names with fried (peace). Painter Frida Kahlo made it known across the Americas.
namesakes: Frida Kahlo (Mexican painter)
Frida Lyngstad (ABBA singer, billed as Frida)

assoc.t: Frida Kahlo, Mexican painter known for self-portraits
Frida, maker of the NoseFrida and other baby-care products

e.etymology: Used in the US almost entirely after R&B singer Jhene Aiko, who says it juh-NAY. The spelling sits close to Janae and Jenae, modern American names in the Jane family.
namesakes: Jhene Aiko (R&B singer)

assoc.t: Jhene Aiko, R&B singer

e.note: Often misread as JEEN or JEN; the intended sound is juh-NAY.

e.etymology: A Danish short form of Katherine that arose in the Middle Ages and reached America with Scandinavian settlers. Katherine is Greek Aikaterine, long linked to katharos (pure). Karen was a top-ten US name in the 1950s and 1960s.
namesakes: Karen Carpenter (singer of the Carpenters)
Karen Gillan (actress, Guardians of the Galaxy)

assoc.t: Karen, slang for an entitled, complaining woman
the Karen, an ethnic group of Myanmar and Thailand

e.note: Karen is now a widely used insult for an entitled, demanding woman, and use of the name has fallen sharply.

e.etymology: From French Desiree (desired), the feminine of the saint's name Desiderius. Desiree Clary, once engaged to Napoleon, became queen of Sweden, and a 1954 Hollywood film told her story.

assoc.t: Desiree, the 1977 Neil Diamond song

e.meaning: gift (Slavic); also an Irish saint's name and a Persian royal name
e.etymology: Several unrelated names share this spelling: an Irish saint's name from Daire, a Slavic name from dar (gift), and the Persian Dara, a form of Darius. In Ireland it is often linked with the word for oak.
namesakes: Dara Torres (Olympic swimmer with 12 medals)

e.meaning: carter, one who hauls goods by cart
e.etymology: A French occupational surname for a carter, someone who hauled goods by cart. As a first name it refers to the Paris jewelry house Cartier, founded in 1847.

assoc.t: Cartier, French luxury jeweler and watchmaker
Jacques Cartier, French explorer of Canada

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Camden, an English surname and place name read as Old English camp (enclosure) plus denu (valley). Camden is also a district of London and a city in New Jersey.
The Italian and Spanish form of Zaire, the heroine's name in Voltaire's 1732 tragedy, which Bellini turned into the opera Zaira. Its older source is uncertain; Arabic origins have been proposed.
From Kal-El, Superman's birth name on the planet Krypton in DC Comics, written as one word. It has no meaning outside the comics.

assoc.t: Kal-El, Superman's Kryptonian birth name

e.etymology: The French form of Christina, from Latin Christiana (follower of Christ), the name of an early martyr. The word Christ is Greek for anointed.
namesakes: Christine Baranski (actress, The Good Wife)
Christine McVie (Fleetwood Mac singer-songwriter)
Christine Daae (heroine of The Phantom of the Opera)

assoc.t: Christine, Stephen King's novel about a killer car
Christine Daaé, the soprano of The Phantom of the Opera

e.etymology: Most likely a respelling of Koa with the final h of Noah. Koa is a Hawaiian word for brave or warrior and the name of the native koa tree.
A Scottish surname that began as a pet form of William, also spelled Wiley. Some families take it instead from English place names such as Willey (willow clearing).

assoc.t: Wile E. Coyote of Looney Tunes (sounds the same)

e.note: Sounds the same as wily, meaning cunning, and as Wile E. Coyote.

e.etymology: From a surname with several possible sources, among them the Old Norse name Kori, of uncertain meaning, and the Gaelic word coire (hollow, cauldron). For girls it is also a pet form of Cora and Corinne.
namesakes: Cory Booker (US senator from New Jersey)
Cory Matthews (lead character of Boy Meets World)
Cory Monteith (Glee actor)

assoc.t: Cory Matthews, the lead of Boy Meets World

e.etymology: A spelling of Anaya with the -ah ending of Aaliyah and Amiyah. Anaya has no single source; it is linked to the biblical Hebrew name Anaiah (God has answered) and to Arabic Inaya (care, protection).

Used as a spelling of Marlow or Marlowe, an English place-name surname built on Old English mere (lake, pool). Actress Marlo Thomas, whose name began as a childhood form of Margo, made it familiar in the 1960s.
namesakes: Marlo Thomas (That Girl actress and St. Jude spokeswoman)
Marlo Stanfield (drug kingpin in The Wire)

e.etymology: From the English surname and church title bishop, which goes back through Old English and Latin to Greek episkopos (overseer). The surname was often a nickname for someone who served a bishop or looked like one.

assoc.t: bishop, a senior rank of Christian clergy
bishop, the chess piece that moves diagonally
Bishop, the android in the film Aliens

e.etymology: A name used in Spanish-speaking families whose origin is unclear. It resembles Israel, Ismael and Misael and may have begun as a form of one of them.
The Italian form of Alexius, from Greek Alexios, from alexein (to defend, to help). Saint Alexius of Rome is Sant'Alessio in Italian.
A French pet form of Oda and Ode, short Germanic names from the element od or aud (riches). Odette is the princess turned into a swan in Tchaikovsky's ballet Swan Lake.
namesakes: Odette (the Swan Queen of the ballet Swan Lake)
Odette Annable (actress, Supergirl and House)

assoc.t: Odette, the swan princess of Swan Lake

e.etymology: The English adjective heavenly, from heaven plus -ly, used as a girls' name since the late 20th century alongside Heaven and Nevaeh.

assoc.t: Heavenly, ski resort at Lake Tahoe

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Abraham. Genesis explains it as father of a multitude, the name God gave Abram; scholars also read it as the father is exalted. In the US it is used mainly in Orthodox Jewish families.
The English animal word and the surname taken from it, first a nickname for someone thought sly like a fox. Fox Mulder of The X-Files brought it attention as a first name.
namesakes: Fox Mulder (FBI agent in The X-Files)

assoc.t: Fox, the TV network, and Fox News
Fox Racing, motocross and mountain bike gear
fox, slang for an attractive person

e.etymology: A spelling of Kaylee, a late 20th-century name built from Kay and Lee or taken from the surname Cayley. Kaylee itself reached its US peak in 2009.
A respelling of Addison, an English surname meaning son of Addie, a medieval pet form of Adam. The -syn ending follows spellings like Madisyn and Jordyn.

A French pet form of Bernarde, the feminine of Bernard, a Germanic name from bern (bear) and hard (brave, hardy). Saint Bernadette of Lourdes, who reported visions of the Virgin Mary in 1858, made it a Catholic favorite.
namesakes: Saint Bernadette of Lourdes (French visionary)
Bernadette Peters (Broadway star)
Bernadette Rostenkowski (The Big Bang Theory microbiologist)

assoc.t: Bernadette, the 1967 Four Tops hit

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Zachary, the English form of Hebrew Zekharyah (the Lord has remembered). Zakari is also a usual form of the name in parts of West Africa.

e.meaning: gift of God; also a Yiddish pet form of Joshua
e.etymology: Has two Jewish sources: a Yiddish pet form of Yehoshua (Joshua) that is common in Hasidic families, and a Hebrew name read as gift of God, the meaning actor Shia LaBeouf gives for his own name.
namesakes: Shia LaBeouf (actor, Transformers)

assoc.t: Shia Islam, one of the two main branches of Islam
Shia LaBeouf, actor

e.note: Spelled the same as Shia, the branch of Islam, which is said SHEE-uh.

e.etymology: The Spanish name treated as the equivalent of Roger, a Germanic name from hrod (fame) and ger (spear). Some scholars trace it instead to the Late Latin name Rogelius, borne by a 9th-century martyr of Cordoba.
namesakes: Rogelio De La Vega (telenovela-star father in Jane the Virgin)
